raw_receipt.title: EvalResearchBench: Can AI Agents Build Their Own Feedback for Recursive Self-Improvement?

blocks.text: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on evaluation feedback to assess progress and guide further research, yet repeatedly running complex benchmarks is costly and slows iteration. Human experts reduce this cost by selecting benchmark subsets or designing compact suites. We ask whether AI agents can automate this design process and introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB), a benchmark for autonomous evaluation research. Given target materials, development references, candidate APIs, and fixed time and API budgets, an agent called the researcher selects or synthesizes tasks, implements graders, and revises them in pilot tests before freezing an executable evaluator for coding, co-work, and reasoning. We study 9 researchers and 13 candidate models and compare each frozen evaluator with 14 target benchmarks on score concordance and pairwise agreement. The best evaluators order about 75% of candidate pairs as the targets do, below the 91% ceiling set by disagreements among the targets. No researcher leads on every metric, and the best evaluator on development targets is not the best on sealed targets hidden from the researcher. A human-designed sample of public tasks remains a strong baseline, and the evaluator with the lowest recorded execution cost attains the highest pairwise agreement. Agents repair tasks and graders through pilot feedback, yet their evaluators can still truncate answers, exhaust the evaluation budget, or let a few questions dominate a domain score.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on evaluation feedback to determine whether a change improves a system and which direction to explore next. Each new training recipe, dataset, or program creates another version to assess. Repeatedly running complex benchmarks incurs API and compute costs and delays the next experiment, particularly when evaluation requires long tool-using trajectories or specialized environments. Human experts reduce this burden by selecting representative subsets or designing cheaper proxies, as in tinyBenchmarks ( Maia Polo et al., 2024 ) . An autonomous improvement loop would need to perform this design step itself and obtain feedback that is informative enough to guide decisions and cheap enough to repeat.

Recent work automates improvement while relying on supplied evaluation protocols. In PostTrainBench, agents choose data and post-training algorithms, but the target benchmark and evaluation harness are fixed ( Rank et al., 2026 ) . RSIBench-Data lets agents revise training-data strategies using checkpoint scores and trajectories from a fixed evaluation service ( Meng et al., 2026 ) . AlphaEvolve evolves programs using a user-provided evaluation function, with optional user-specified test cascades to screen proposals efficiently ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) . In each case, humans decide what to test, how to score it, and how to keep repeated measurement affordable, so extending autonomy to a new domain still requires a human-designed evaluation.

Other work automates parts of evaluation design. PACE selects inexpensive source questions and calibrates them against expensive agentic targets ( Song et al., 2026 ) . AutoBencher and BenchAgents automate benchmark construction and refinement ( Li et al., 2025 ; Butt et al., 2025 ) , and BenchBench compares the quality of model-designed suites ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . None of these settings poses the full research problem, in which an agent chooses a measurement strategy, spends a limited experimental budget, and revises an executable evaluator until it tracks complex target benchmarks. Solving it requires inspecting target evidence, choosing or creating tasks, verifying graders, and deciding whether a pilot failure calls for harder questions, different coverage, a repaired rubric, or more execution budget. We therefore ask whether an agent with fixed time and API budgets can build an evaluator that reproduces how complex target benchmarks score and rank models. We call this capability autonomous evaluation research.

To address these gaps, we introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB) , in which the researcher designs the measurement itself, pays for every pilot from a fixed budget, and submits an executable evaluator that is scored against complex target benchmarks. A researcher is a model in an agent harness that designs the evaluator, a candidate is a model being tested, and a target benchmark is an established evaluation whose candidate scores the evaluator should reproduce. The researcher receives target descriptions, permitted tasks and grading resources, execution traces, development reference scores, and APIs for development candidates (Figure 2 ). In pilot tests, it observes candidate responses, costs, and agreement with the visible references, then revises its tasks, graders, weights, and answer allowances. It then freezes an evaluator that returns one score per domain. Sealed candidates and targets stay hidden during research, so the researcher can neither call those candidates nor see those reference scores. Independent assessment runs the frozen evaluator on all candidates under a separate budget and compares its scores with both development and sealed targets.

Figure 2: EvalResearchBench. Research materials support an autonomous design–test–revise loop. Tasks, graders, and score weights are frozen before independent assessment. Candidate-model and target visibility are assigned separately.

We evaluate 9 researcher configurations, each a model in the Codex or Claude Code harness run for one episode, on 13 open-weight and proprietary candidates and 14 target benchmarks in coding, co-work, and reasoning (Table 1 ). These domains cover the implementation, professional work, and analysis that autonomous research relies on. As a baseline, Random120 samples public tasks under fixed source quotas designed by humans.

We measure agreement in two ways. Score is 100 times Lin’s concordance correlation coefficient between measured and reference scores ( Lin, 1989 ) , so it rewards matching score level and spread as well as order. Pairwise agreement (PA) is the fraction of candidate pairs that the evaluator orders as the target does. We also separate the one-time cost of building an evaluator from the cost of running it, which recurs for every new candidate.

No evaluator leads in every domain (Figure 1 ). Grok 4.7 leads coding, Astra leads co-work, and Opus 5 leads reasoning, while coding is the weakest domain for most evaluators. Astra attains the highest overall Score and Grok 4.7 the highest PA. Even the best PA, about 75%, stays well below the 91% ceiling set by disagreements among the targets. Fable 5.1 has the highest Score on development targets but not on sealed ones, so fitting visible references does not ensure transfer. Random120 remains a strong baseline. On identical candidates, seven of eight agent-designed evaluators exceed it in Score, but only four exceed it in PA. Evaluators with similar construction cost differ markedly in execution cost, and the one with the lowest recorded execution cost attains the highest PA. Agents repair tasks and graders through pilot feedback, yet their final evaluators can still truncate answers, exhaust the assessment budget, or let a few heavily weighted questions dominate a domain score.

Evaluation design spans coverage and standardization ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ; Liang et al., 2023 ; Kiela et al., 2021 ) , task construction ( Perez et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023a ; Xia et al., 2024 ) , and automated grading ( Liu et al., 2023c ; Zheng et al., 2023 ) . AutoBencher refines datasets using model feedback ( Li et al., 2025 ) ; BenchAgents integrates planning, generation, verification, and evaluation ( Butt et al., 2025 ) ; BenchBench assesses benchmark designers through validity, discrimination, and ranking reliability ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Efficient measurement offers another route: APTBench transforms agent tasks and trajectories into lightweight questions ( Qin et al., 2025 ) , while tinyBenchmarks, Fluid Benchmarking, and Efficient Benchmarking of AI Agents study selection, estimation, and adaptive testing ( Maia Polo et al., 2024 ; Hofmann et al., 2025 ; Ndzomga, 2026 ) . Agent Psychometrics models task-level performance from task and system features ( Ge et al., 2026 ) . ERB evaluates an agent’s ability to choose and develop measurement strategies through autonomous, budgeted experimentation.

Research benchmarks study iterative experimentation ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Nathani et al., 2025 ) , resource-bounded machine-learning research ( Chan et al., 2025 ; Wijk et al., 2025 ) , replication ( Starace et al., 2025 ) , and post-training ( Rank et al., 2026 ) . The AI Scientist and Agent Laboratory integrate multiple stages of scientific work ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Schmidgall et al., 2025 ) . Self-improvement systems such as FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, and the Darwin Gödel Machine use evaluation feedback to guide program or agent revisions ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ; Novikov et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) ; MIRROR and TRIAGE study self-knowledge and resource allocation ( Wang, 2026 ; Nazi & Dipta, 2026 ) . ERB focuses on constructing the feedback instrument itself. Following artifact-based research benchmarks, it assesses the submitted evaluation independently of the process that produced it.

The researcher is an LLM agent equipped with a harness that lets it inspect files, write and execute code, call models, and revise its work. A candidate is a model–execution configuration whose capabilities the researcher must measure. A target benchmark provides the reference candidate scores that the resulting evaluation should reproduce.

We cover three complementary capabilities needed for autonomous research. Coding supports implementing and testing systems, from repository engineering to scientific programming and terminal workflows ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Tian et al., 2024a ; Merrill et al., 2026 ) . Co-work covers gathering information, following constraints, and producing professional deliverables ( He et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Patwardhan et al., 2025 ) . Reasoning covers analytical work with academic questions, long documents, and specialized physics ( Phan et al., 2025 ; Artificial Analysis, 2025a ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . A single research episode designs an evaluation across all three domains, allowing the agent to share resources and choose where further testing is most useful.

We provide target descriptions, available original tasks and grading resources, historical execution traces, and reference scores for development candidates. The researcher also receives metered candidate-model APIs, an execution SDK, and the submission contract. Resource availability varies by target; the agent may select existing tasks, synthesize new ones, or combine both approaches. Development tests return candidate responses and grading results for diagnosing errors and improving correlation with the visible target references.

We constrain three costs: researcher inference pays for the agent’s analysis and tool use; development testing pays for candidate and helper-model calls; independent assessment pays to execute the frozen design. Keeping the first two budgets separate prevents agent deliberation from consuming the testing allowance. A fixed deadline limits research time. Section 4.1 gives the numerical limits.

The researcher may select, synthesize, or simplify tasks, repair graders, change task weights, set answer allowances, and inspect pilot responses. Calls and retries pass through a metered gateway. The agent allocates its development budget across exploration, testing, and revision without a prescribed sequence.

To require a reusable test suite rather than a few demonstrations, the agent submits at least 100 distinct scored questions, together with executable graders and fixed aggregation rules. The program returns one measured score per domain from candidate responses and frozen assets, without candidate-identity lookup or access to reference labels during scoring. Questions, grading code, and weights are frozen before assessment. One ERB entry is one research episode by a particular model and harness.

To test transfer beyond development feedback, we execute the frozen program independently on development and withheld candidates and compare its scores with visible and withheld target references. Candidate access and target-reference access are assigned separately (Table 1 ).

The executor records per-item rewards, termination reasons, and usage. A total assessment cap limits the cost of evaluating the candidate panel, while a per-candidate cap bounds the cost of applying the design to any one model. Assessment is charged separately from development, and its results are not returned to the researcher for further revision.

A graded response is complete under the submitted contract, including a wrong or empty answer at the output cap. Infrastructure failures and budget-stopped items remain incomplete. We compare how different LLM researchers use the available materials and budget to build evaluations. The experiments first assess the resulting measurements, then examine the design choices and costs behind them. Appendix E traces how these choices arise during research.

We study nine researcher configurations: GPT-6 Astra ( OpenAI, 2026c ) , GPT-5.6 Sol ( OpenAI, 2026b ) , GLM-5.3 ( Z.ai, 2026b ) , DeepSeek V4 Pro ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 ) , Kimi K3 ( Kimi Team et al., 2026 ) , Fable 5.1 ( Anthropic, 2026b ) , Opus 5 ( Anthropic, 2026c ) , Grok 4.7 ( xAI, 2026 ) , and Fable 5 ( Anthropic, 2026a ) . Each contributes one research episode. The GPT researchers and Grok use Codex ( OpenAI, 2025a ) ; the other researchers use Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2025 ) . The candidate panel contains four development-visible and nine sealed models (Table 1 ).

The research budget is three hours, $100 for researcher inference, and $100 for shared development/helper testing. Independent assessment has a $120 total cap and a $30 per-candidate cap. Pilots may use smaller suites than the final submission; the researcher allocates its development calls freely.

A research agent should be compared with a simpler way to build a broad evaluation: sample questions from existing public sources. We use Random120 , a source-stratified baseline that fixes the number of questions drawn from each source, ensuring coverage across task types before sampling. Specifically, we select sixteen public task sources, eligibility filters, source quotas, local graders, and equal item weighting within each domain. A seeded draw within each source selects 40 coding, 40 co-work, and 40 reasoning tasks without using target reference scores. We assess its twelve complete candidates against the same fourteen targets (Appendix B.1 ).

Eight submissions yield all 39 candidate-domain scores. Fable 5 reaches its assessment budget before completing the panel; Table 2 reports its stated imputation scenario separately from the eight observed-score results.

Astra leads overall Score, whereas Grok leads PA: reproducing score levels and recovering candidate order favor different designs. Domain strengths also vary, with no researcher dominating both metrics across all three domains. Decomposing CCC as r ​ C b rC_{b} helps explain why: Astra and GLM-5.3 have similar co-work correlations, but Astra aligns more closely with the reference scale (Table 10 ). A useful ordering alone does not guarantee faithful score reproduction.

Fable 5.1 leads development Score, but Grok leads sealed Score. This reversal makes cross-target transfer a distinct requirement for evaluation research: a useful design must preserve capability signals beyond the references used to develop it. Systematic score shifts across targets within the same domain (Figure 7 ) further show why a strong fit to one benchmark does not establish a broadly useful evaluator.

Random120’s public sources, domain quotas, and graders encode task-design knowledge, making it a strong baseline, especially in coding. Its coding and reasoning coverage recovers much of the candidate ordering, while Astra’s Score gains concentrate in co-work and reasoning (Figure 3 ). DeepSeek V4 Pro illustrates why iteration alone need not beat this baseline. It revises coding tasks and increases reasoning allowances, yet its short, deterministic coding and co-work checks yield scores clustered near the ceiling; its reasoning gains cannot offset the coding deficit. Research adds value when it identifies tasks that preserve target-relevant differences between candidates. Ease of grading and repeated revision do not by themselves ensure informative measurements.

Figure 3: Where research differs from fixed public-task sampling. Differences from Random120 on identical candidate–target intersections: (a) per domain; (b) overall, with central 95% candidate-resampling ranges. The twelve candidates are jointly resampled; fourteen targets and frozen evaluations stay fixed.
We analyze three design decisions—task selection, question count, and aggregation—by varying one part of each evaluation while holding candidate responses and references fixed.

K3 adds hard coding problems after near-ceiling pilots; Astra adds repository traces after inspecting upstream software tasks. Removing these groups, however, has only modest effects relative to same-domain, same-size random deletions. K3’s addition improves Score but slightly reduces PA; Astra’s repository group leaves PA unchanged. By contrast, Astra’s spreadsheet tasks contribute strongly to both co-work metrics (Figure 4 a,b). Task realism and difficulty motivate a design, but its value depends on how it separates candidates in relation to the target.

Many Astra spreadsheet responses exhaust their answer allowance, so the observed separation reflects the task under its chosen execution conditions. Grok responds to truncated hard-task pilots by favoring shorter, self-contained checks and adjusting answer allowances. DeepSeek instead expands reasoning allowances and selects short exact-answer items. A short expected answer does not itself make a problem easy to solve.

Figure 4: Task contribution and measurement variability. (a,b) Full-minus-deleted Score and PA for seven task groups; parentheses give question counts. Gray intervals cover the central 95% of 1,000 same-domain, same-size random deletions. (c,d) Mean overall Score and PA across nested question subsets, with central 95% bands. (e,f) Their standard deviations. Candidates, targets, and responses are fixed.

We draw nested, domain-stratified subsets from the frozen Astra, GLM-5.3, and K3 suites and recompute their scores on the same candidate panel. As subsets grow, mean Score rises and both Score and PA fluctuate less across question draws (Figure 4 c–f). Small subsets can omit useful task families or overrepresent a few responses, even when their domain proportions are fixed. The design problem is to retain this signal and consistency with fewer calls.

Grok groups pilot questions by which development candidates pass, then searches for weights that reproduce the visible ordering and score gaps. For co-work, it assigns most weight to questions that all three tested development candidates pass, using a small remainder to shape their differences. Consequently, six of its twenty co-work questions carry almost all scoring weight. Fable 5.1 distributes influence more evenly, with a modest upweighting of professional tasks (Figure 5 a).

Recomputing Grok’s scores with equal item weights on the same responses substantially improves coding and co-work Score, while overall PA barely changes (Figure 5 ). The Score improvement also holds on the complete-item candidate subset. The frozen suite therefore contains useful measurement signal that its chosen weights underuse. Evaluation design must consider task contribution, sampling variability, and score aggregation jointly.

Figure 5: Weight allocation and measurement quality. Grok and Fable (Fable 5.1) use their submitted weights. (a) Cumulative co-work weight versus the fraction of questions, sorted by decreasing weight; the dashed diagonal denotes uniform weighting. (b,c) Score and PA on the same twelve-candidate, fourteen-target panel. Here Uniform weights reweights Grok’s grades only; connectors show this change, with its responses and item exclusions fixed.

An evaluator is built once but may be run repeatedly, so we separate construction cost from frozen assessment cost. Grok combines low assessment cost with the highest overall PA and a competitive Score (Figure 6 ; Table 2 ). Grok and Fable 5.1 submit similar question counts, yet their execution costs differ substantially. Task count alone therefore gives little indication of an evaluator’s recurring cost.

Figure 6: Spending and measurement quality. Overall Score against recorded API-equivalent costs for (a) researcher inference plus development tests and (b) frozen assessment. Solid markers use metered usage; hollow markers use collaborator reports. Unresolved reservations are excluded.

Grok’s hard HLE pilots exhaust their answer allowance without producing visible answers. It responds by favoring short code, output predictions, and numeric checks with local graders. Fable 5.1 retains longer professional deliverables and increases their answer allowance after truncated pilots; its rubric judge adds a substantial second expense. Opus incurs little grading expense but still spends heavily on candidate answers. These trajectories identify two distinct design choices behind execution cost: what a candidate must produce and how its answer is judged (Appendix A.3 ).

Researchers use development feedback to expand coverage, repair tasks, and adjust execution. Astra develops repository-tracing tasks from source inspection, resolves prompt–rubric mismatches through pilot feedback, and adjusts execution after truncated responses. GLM corrects invalid examples and numerical answers, while K3 adds harder coding tasks after near-ceiling pilot scores. Section 4.3 analyzes these design choices; Appendix E details the cases.

ERB measures autonomous evaluation research under fixed budgets. Independent assessment separates score reproduction, ordering, and execution cost. Source inspection and pilot audits reveal how agents revise tasks and graders; component and subset analyses show why difficulty, nominal size, and measurement value must be assessed separately. This establishes an executable benchmark for the evaluation-design capability that autonomous improvement requires.

A single domain score can therefore preserve different aspects of different targets.

Reference targets in one domain sometimes order the same candidate pair differently. We calculate the largest PA attainable by any single strict candidate ordering per domain on the fixed panel. Every target and every non-tied pair within it receives exactly the weight used in Section 3.3 ; an exact subset dynamic program maximizes the weighted agreement. A measured tie earns the average of its two possible orientations and cannot improve the optimum. This label-informed oracle is an upper bound for a frozen evaluator, not a deployable score:
Domain Development Sealed Overall

Each column optimizes its own target set, so the overall maximum need not average the development and sealed maxima. Cross-target order conflicts cap overall PA at 91.20%, compared with the best observed artifact’s 74.87%.

Fable 5 produced 20 of 39 candidate-domain reports before assessment stopped at the budget cap. The main ranking excludes it. Table 2 separately reports the fixed scenario that assigns its 19 unobserved domain scores a value of one; these are scenario-conditional metrics, not observed-panel estimates or metric bounds.

Fable 5.1 grades GDPval against upstream rubric criteria using helper-grader ; its free-response reasoning uses local matching followed, when needed, by helper-simulator . The corresponding known assessment charges are $33.9709 and $0.0070. Fable 5 uses the same division of grader roles, with up to three rubric-judge attempts when a verdict cannot be parsed ($18.0167 rubric and $0.0038 equivalence charges). Opus uses deterministic structural/numeric checks for co-work and only the cheap reasoning equivalence path ($0.0193). Grok has no assessment helper calls. These partitions reconcile to the framework’s recorded evaluation totals; outstanding reservations remain separate at $7.1444, $1.9747, and $7.6783 for the three supplied runs.

Fable 5.1’s early valid snapshots contain 145–153 items including ArXivMath ( Dekoninck et al., 2026 ) . Its pilot tool outputs record empty capped ArXivMath responses on both tested candidates. Later snapshots remove that family and reduce the suite to 110 items. A completed development pass then records nine capped GDPval answers out of sixteen, prompting a final increase from 8,000 to 16,000 tokens for that family. Opus’s development diagnostic records 36 capped responses out of 102, including 32 empty replies; its final code increases reasoning, coding, and co-work caps to 24,000, 16,000, and 8,000. These diagnostics establish why the researchers changed the settings, without assuming the larger caps necessarily improve every final metric.

Fable 5’s trajectory shows that grading is also part of the iteration budget. Its rubric helper initially exhausts its allowance without a parsable verdict; the researcher increases that allowance, adds bounded retry samples, and changes error handling to preserve other item results. Slow candidate calls and late grading failures delay the response matrix needed for weight selection, so the final suite retains its predefined family weights. Monetary spend, feedback latency, and deployment cost are therefore distinct constraints on evaluation research.

Random120 tests how much agreement can be obtained by sampling existing public tasks without iterative research. We fix source-level quotas to cover multiple task types, then sample within each source independently of target reference scores. The maintainers selected sixteen sources, screened 21,083 eligible items, set source quotas, adapted fixed local graders, and used equal item weights for each raw domain mean. A Python pseudorandom generator with seed 42 sampled only within each source. Coding draws eight tasks each from MBPP ( Austin et al., 2021 ) , HumanEval ( Chen et al., 2021 ) , DebugBench ( Tian et al., 2024b ) , LiveCodeBench ( Jain et al., 2025 ) , and RepoBench ( Liu et al., 2023b ) . Reasoning draws ten each from LogiQA ( Liu et al., 2020 ) , MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) , GPQA ( Rein et al., 2023 ) , and AIME25 ( Balunovic et al., 2026 ) . The resulting frozen suite has 40 tasks per domain, 120 in total. Twelve candidates completed all three domains, yielding 7–11 matched candidate scores per target across fourteen references. DeepSeek’s source inspection identifies deterministic grading as a practical way to keep evaluation inexpensive. It constructs Python output-prediction, function-writing, and bug-fixing tasks, plus co-work checks for specified text, numbers, and formats. For example, one co-work question asks for a letter count but supplies the required output string; another asks for time conversion and supplies the converted time. Such checks measure compliance with an explicit response more directly than independent professional problem solving.

The trajectory includes genuine revisions: coding tasks are hardened, a domain-name mismatch in feedback analysis is repaired, and truncated reasoning pilots lead to larger answer allowances and a different question mix. The final reasoning bank includes short-answer HLE questions whose expected answers are easy to parse but whose mathematical content remains demanding. Selecting a short answer simplifies grading, not necessarily reasoning. Final item counts are 38 coding, 51 co-work, and 30 reasoning, with equal within-domain weights.

On the matched panel, DeepSeek’s coding and co-work means are high and its concordance calibration factors are low (Table 10 ). Its reasoning Score exceeds Random120’s, whereas coding accounts for the largest deficit (Table 9 ). These observations support the interpretation that simplifying task form can preserve answer checkability while compressing the capability differences the proxy is intended to recover. They do not isolate task content from grading and execution as separate causal interventions.

Researchers are asked to design one executable evaluation with at least 100 distinct scored questions spanning coding, co-work, and reasoning. They may select, adapt, or synthesize tasks and choose graders, weights, grouping, and output allowances. During development, researchers compare directly measured candidate-domain scores with visible target-reference scores; final assessment reports Score and PA for frozen programs.

The supplied workspace contains the task contract, development candidate APIs and available reference scores, original benchmark materials, available trajectories, and a Python evaluation SDK. The SDK submits a suite, records item-level responses and costs, and returns cross-model feedback on completed development tests. Researchers decide what to test, revise, and freeze within the three-hour research period, $100 researcher wallet, and $100 shared development/helper wallet. Frozen assessment has a separate $120 wallet and $30 per-candidate cap.

The final program supplies executable questions, grading rules, and three fixed domain aggregations. Completed wrong or empty answers retain their grades; infrastructure failures remain incomplete. After freezing, the executor runs the candidate panel without sending assessment results back to the researcher.

The aggregate analyses show which design choices affect measurement, but do not explain how agents arrive at them. We now follow the saved research trajectories from source inspection through pilot testing and revision. Astra provides a concrete example of this loop; GLM and K3 illustrate different responses to development feedback.

A compact coding evaluation can miss repository-level behavior if it concentrates on isolated implementations. After inspecting upstream repository-investigation tasks, Astra identifies a gap in its implementation-heavy coding bank and constructs eight multi-file repository traces. In one, candidates predict cached outputs and recomputation counts after in-place mutation versus replacing a dependency object. Running the supplied fixture generates the expected outputs for grading (Figure 13 a).

A low pilot score may expose an unclear question or an overly restrictive grader, as well as a candidate error. Astra examines these possibilities in a performance-plan memo that scores 11/12: its response reports that 3/13 orders finish on time, but omits the mean close time required by the rubric. Astra finds that the question never explicitly requested that statistic and adds it to the brief. A later audit also relaxes a cloud-migration rubric that prescribed one architecture despite an open-ended brief, retaining the stated security and delivery requirements (Figure 13 b,c). These revisions align prompts and graders before freezing; the saved pilot score precedes the repairs.

GLM corrects invalid examples and numerical answers; K3 responds to near-ceiling pilots with five hard coding tasks. Astra also changes answer allowances and grouped execution after truncated responses. These examples show three uses of pilot feedback: correcting task validity, extending coverage, and changing execution settings. The component analysis in Section 4.3 tests whether the resulting task groups improve agreement on the frozen candidate panel.
